abstract.p: Niosomes are known to improve the bioavailability of drugs. However, niosomes have drawbacks related to stability and absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Chitosan coating on niosomes can increase their stability in gastrointestinal fluid and absorption after oral administration. This study aimed to evaluate the biopharmaceutical stability and oral absorption of chitosan-coated Ursolic acid niosomes in vivo. Niosomes Ursolic Acid (Nio-UA) were prepared using a thin-layer hydration method, and chitosan was added to produce Niosomes Ursolic Acid with chitosan coating (Nio-UA-CS). The stability of niosomes was evaluated by exposing them to simulated gastrointestinal fluid. The oral absorption and biodistribution were determined in vivo. The results showed that niosome formation increased UA solubility from 1.02 × 10–4 mg/mL to 23.49 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA and 22.34 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA-CS and decreased the LogP value of UA from 5.18 ± 0.05 to 1.70 ± 0.22 for Nio-UA and 1.74 ± 0.30 for Nio-UA-CS. Adding chitosan layers increased the stability of the niosome, resulting in the lowest %cumulative calcein release of 7.05 ± 1.77% in Nio-UA-CS after exposure to simulated gastric fluid and 31.53 ± 8.80% after exposure to simulated intestinal fluid. Chitosan-coated niosomes exhibited higher absorption in the duodenum. Moreover, photomicrographs revealed that UA niosomes with a chitosan layer were highly accumulated in the liver 4 h after oral administration. A biodistribution study revealed that chitosan coating increased the plasma concentration of UA and selective hepatic accumulation. Thus, the chitosan layer successfully improved the oral absorption of UA niosomes, providing potential uses of nanoparticles for improving drugs’ bioavailability.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Currently, the medium of drug delivery for chemotherapy is predominantly via the oral administration route [1] due to patient preference and lower manufacturing costs than those of other administration routes [2]. Compared to the intravenous route, oral chemotherapy can maintain continuous drug delivery. Intravenous administration allows plasma drug levels to exceed the effective levels and achieve faster drug clearance [3]. With the development of many chemotherapy drugs, patients tend to prefer oral chemotherapy over intravenous chemotherapy despite having the same efficacy and toxicity [4]. In addition, oral chemotherapy is an important step towards comprehending patients’ desire for “chemotherapy at home,” which will greatly improve their quality of life. Unfortunately, most anticancer drugs exhibit poor bioavailability. Thus, it is necessary to develop an optimal drug delivery system for oral cancer therapy that can overcome the low solubility and permeability of active ingredients and reduce the side effects of chemotherapy drugs.

Ursolic acid (UA) is a potential chemotherapeutic drug used in patients with liver cancer. UA belongs to the pentacyclic triterpenoid compound group [5]. This compound is highly abundant in medicinal plants and several fruits and vegetables, suggesting its therapeutic potential [5, 6]. The mechanism of action of UA in cancer therapy involves the inhibition of tumorigenesis and cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis induction via the mitochondria-mediated pathway [7, 8].

However, UA is included in the Bioavailability Classification System (BCS) class IV. This drug has a low solubility of 1.02 × 10–4 mg/mL and poor permeability (LogP = 7.92) [9–11]. The low water solubility of UA can potentially affect treatment effectiveness. Low drug solubility limits its bioavailability in the body on oral administration, whereas low drug permeability reduces its ability for intestinal absorption [12]. Thus, the poor solubility and permeability of UA limit its clinical use in cancer therapy. Therefore, the development of a drug delivery system for UA is necessary to increase its bioavailability.

Vesicle-based drug delivery systems, such as liposomes and niosomes, are commonly used in drug delivery for cancer therapy. This system can encapsulate both hydrophilic and hydrophobic drugs and increase their solubility and permeability [13]. Liposomes are spherical nanoparticles consisting of one or more phospholipid layers. However, the liposomal system is prone to degradation by gastric acid and other enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract [14]. In addition, phospholipids accelerate the phagocytosis of liposomes when entering systemic circulation [15]. Thus, liposomes are rarely used for oral drug delivery.

Niosomes are promising, novel drug delivery systems for oral administration. Niosomes are vesicular nanocarriers that can trap hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds [16]. This system is similar to liposomes but differs in the bilayer composition, wherein niosomes are composed of non-ionic surfactants and cholesterol in an aqueous phase. Although the physical and biopharmaceutical properties of niosomes are similar, niosomes possess advantages, such as better stability in the digestive tract, easier handling and storage, and lower costs [17, 18]. Drug formulations in niosomes can increase drug solubility and permeability through encapsulation in hydrophilic and hydrophobic groups [19]. The encapsulation of UA in a niosome bilayer membrane occurs through interaction with the alkyl chain of the surfactant. The hydrophilic polar group on the outside of the niosome forms hydrogen bonds with water, thereby increasing drug solubility [20, 21]. The permeability of niosomes is increased by forming a bilayer membrane with the noisome components, namely Span 60 and cholesterol, thus increasing drug partitioning [22]. The niosome system increases bioavailability by crossing the digestive tract barrier and increasing the solubility and permeability of poorly absorbed drugs [23]. In addition, this system is more stable against chemical degradation and oxidation and can extend the circulation time of drugs [19, 24]. Thus, the formulation of UA in the niosome system can enhance its potential as an oral chemotherapeutic agent.

It is challenging to formulate an oral drug delivery system, as exposure to the gastrointestinal environment can affect drug integrity in the system. Oral vesicular-based drug delivery systems are susceptible to physiological factors, such as gastric acid, bile salts, and lipases [25], which can have a destructive effect, resulting in loss of membrane integrity and cargo leakage due to disruption of the bilayer membrane structure [26]. Moreover, pH variations in the gastrointestinal tract also affect the absorption and bioavailability of oral drugs since they can cause degradation of the carrier system owing to protonation, such as in the liposome system [27]. Thus, it is necessary to ensure that the system is stable during entry into the digestive tract and can pass through the gastrointestinal tract barrier to be absorbed into systemic circulation.

Furthermore, oral drug absorption is a complex process influenced by many factors related to the physicochemical properties of the drug, the nature of the dosage form, and the physiology of the gastrointestinal tract [2]. Drug absorption from the gastrointestinal tract can vary significantly owing to variability in physiological factors, which affect absorption along the gastrointestinal tract [2]. Oral drugs are maximally absorbed in the small intestine, which includes the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, owing to the presence of villi and microvilli, which increase the surface area by 30–600 times [28]. The duodenum has the largest surface area in the digestive tract since it has more villi and microvilli than those in the jejunum and ileum [29, 30]. Furthermore, mucus and phospholipid layers on the surface of the digestive tract epithelium can inhibit the entry of external foreign objects and molecules [31–33]. These two barriers complicate the absorption of drugs with poor permeability into systemic circulation. Therefore, the surface modification of nanoparticles may potentially increase their stability and absorption in the digestive tract.

Chitosan is a linear amino polysaccharide obtained by the deacetylation of chitin, which can be used for the surface modification of nanoparticles [34]. The mechanism of chitosan coating on the niosome membrane involves the electrostatic interaction of positively charged chitosan with the negatively charged niosome surface [35]. This coating can form a wall, which inhibits the development of the system and prevents the release of encapsulated active ingredients [36]. Chitosan has strong bioadhesive characteristics at a physiological pH. It enhances penetration by forming ionic bonds between the positively charged amino group and the negatively charged cell surface, which provides a mucoadhesive effect [18, 37]. Therefore, this compound can increase residence time and drug permeability in the digestive tract. Furthermore, chitosan can open the tight junctions of intestinal epithelial cells and produce a paracellular pathway through the epithelial barrier to increase systemic penetration [38]. Thus, chitosan coating of oral drugs can increase the absorption of niosomes into the systemic bloodstream through tight junctions, consequently increasing drug absorption into systemic circulation.

The development of oral chemotherapy using UA niosomes (Nio-UA) has been previously reported [39], demonstrating good physical stability with a mole ratio of 3:2:10 for span 60:cholesterol: UA. The addition of chitosan to the UA niosome formulation, UA niosomes with a chitosan coating (Nio-UA-CS), can further increase physical stability, with no sediment formation after storage for 14 days [39]. According to qualitative analysis by Miatmoko et al., Nio-UA-CS accumulate in the liver [39]. The efficacy evaluation of UA niosomes revealed that the presence of chitosan coating increases its effectiveness by reducing serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase and serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase levels and improving the histopathology of liver tissue, which is better than that of negative controls [40]. The formulation of UA niosomes with good in vitro and in vivo stability and absorption can be further developed for high-throughput mass production in other dosage forms with improved storage stability.

In this study, we aimed to evaluate the effects of UA niosome formation with or without chitosan coating on the biopharmaceutical characteristics, stability, absorption, and oral biodistribution of UA. The evaluations included solubility and permeability tests of UA, in vitro stability of UA niosomes with or without chitosan coating in simulated gastric fluid (SGF) and simulated intestinal fluid (SIF) media, degree of in vivo absorption of UA niosomes following oral administration, and drug biodistribution in experimental animals with liver cancer.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: The materials used in this study were as follows: ursolic acid (UA) with a purity degree of ≥90% (Sigma-Aldrich, Tokyo, Japan), cholesterol (Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd., Osaka, Japan), Span 60 (Wako Pure Chemical Industries), Chitosan 19 cps (Biotech, Cirebon, Indonesia), L-α-phosphatidylcholine (Sigma-Aldrich), chloroform p.a (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany), methanol pro high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; Merck), gold nanoparticles (Sigma-Aldrich), Nile Red (Sigma-Aldrich), simulated gastric fluid (SGF) containing NaCl (Merck), pepsin (Sigma-Aldrich), and HCl (Merck), simulated intestinal fluid (SIF)-containing monopotassium phosphate (Sigma-Aldrich) and pancreatin (Sigma-Aldrich), sodium taurocholate (Sigma-Aldrich), n-octanol (Sigma-Aldrich), calcein (Nacalai Tesque Inc, Kyoto, Japan), Tween (Sigma-Aldrich), and Triton™ X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich). Unless otherwise stated, all reagents and materials used were of non-technical grade.

sec.title: Preparation of UA niosomes
sec.p:
UA was encapsulated in niosomes using a thin-layer hydration method. The components of the UA niosomes were first dissolved in organic solvents; cholesterol and Span 60 were dissolved in chloroform, whereas UA was dissolved in methanol. Span 60, cholesterol, and UA were mixed in a round-bottom flask in specific amounts according to the formula in Table 1. Subsequently, evaporation was performed using a rotary evaporator for 60 min at 60 °C. Further, the mixture was homogenized by vortexing and sonicated in a water bath at 60 °C for 30 min to downsize the UA niosomes formed. Centrifugation was performed at 1000 rpm for 10 min to separate free UA from that encapsulated in niosomes. Subsequently, a 0.1% v/v chitosan solution was prepared in 0.1 M acetic acid, which was then diluted using PBS pH 7.4 to obtain a concentration of 0.005% v/v. The chitosan solution was added to UA niosomes at a chitosan: UA niosome volume ratio of 1:10 and vortexed to produce chitosan-coated UA niosomes. The samples were then evaluated for particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency.

sec.title: Characteristics of UA niosomes
sec.p: To characterize UA niosomes, 150 μL of the sample was diluted to 3 mL using water for injection and evaluated using dynamic light scattering to determine the particle size and PDI. Evaluation of ζ-Potential was performed via the electrophoresis light scattering method using the Delsa Nano C Particle Analyzer (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, USA).

sec.title: Determination of encapsulation efficiency
sec.p: A standard curve of UA was generated using a 1000 µg/mL stock solution of UA in methanol. Furthermore, a working standard solution of UA was prepared in a range of 6–120 µg/mL using methanol. The solution was then filtered using a 0.2-µm membrane filter and was used to generate a standard curve of UA. Both standards and samples were prepared using methanol as the solvent. The standard curve and extracted samples were analyzed under the same conditions. To evaluate the encapsulation efficiency, the free and encapsulated UA were separated by centrifugation at a low speed of 1000 rpm for 10 min at 25 °C, specifically optimized for density-based separation of free UA from niosomal vesicles. Free UA sedimented at the bottom of the centrifuge tube, whereas UA niosomes were dispersed in the supernatant. The supernatant was collected to evaluate the level of UA trapped in the niosomes. Drug extraction was performed to break down the niosome system by adding methanol to the UA niosome solution at a ratio of 1:2 (v/v) UA niosome in methanol. Further, the solution was sonicated for 5–10 min at 25 °C until completely dissolved. The sample was then filtered using a 0.2-µm membrane filter and analyzed using HPLC.

sec.title: Solubility assay
sec.p: Solubility was evaluated as previously described by Telange et al. [41]. A total of 1 mg of UA, Nio-UA, and Nio-UA-CS formulations equivalent to 1 mg of UA in 1 mL PBS were added to 4 mL of water in a closed vial at room temperature (25 ± 0.5 °C). The samples were stirred for 2, 6, or 24 h. Further, centrifugation was performed at 1000 rpm for 10 min at 25 °C to separate free UA. The supernatant was collected and used to analyze Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS; drug extraction was performed to lyse the niosome system by adding methanol to the Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS solutions at a ratio of 1:2 (v/v) UA niosomes in methanol. Further, sonication was performed for 5–10 min at 25 °C until completely dissolved. The sample was then filtered using a 0.2-µm membrane filter and analyzed using HPLC. UA has low water solubility (1.02 × 10–4 mg/L) [9, 10]. The increase in solubility is indicated by an increase in UA levels in the aqueous phase after formulation as niosomes [41].

sec.title: Permeability (LogP) determination
sec.p: Permeability was evaluated using a method previously described by Rosita et al. [42] via partition coefficient evaluation of encapsulated UA within a niosome. The partition coefficient value was determined using phosphate buffer pH 7.4 ± 0.05 saturated with n-octanol as the water phase and n-octanol as the oil phase, and the mixture was stirred using a magnetic stirrer. A niosome formula suspension equivalent to UA (1 mg/mL in PBS, pH 7.4) was placed in a glass vial, and 1.0 mL of n-octanol solution was added as the organic phase, which was saturated with PBS pH 7.4. The mixture was then stirred with a magnetic stirrer at 150 rpm and 37 ± 0.5 °C for 30 min. The aqueous phase was separated from the organic phase by centrifuging the sample for 10 min at 1000 rpm. The UA levels in the water and octanol phases were quantified using HPLC. UA exhibits a high LogP value of 7.92 [11]. A decrease in the LogP value indicates an increase in the permeability of UA [42].

sec.title: In vitro analysis of niosome stability
sec.p: The stability of UA niosomes with and without chitosan coating in the digestive tract was evaluated by measuring the release of calcein encapsulated in the niosomes. For comparison, a UA liposome system was constructed using a previously reported formula [38]. Liposomes are composed of L-α-phosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and UA (in a weight ratio of 50:6:5). In this test, calcein was used as a marker in the vesicles at a concentration of 3.4 mM. Leakage of calcein from the vesicles resulted in increased fluorescence, further suggesting that the niosome system, as a carrier, was unstable in the presence of in vitro simulation media. The sample was then inserted into simulated gastric fluid (SGF) consisting of 0.2% NaCl, 0.2% pepsin, and 0.7% HCl, and the pH was adjusted to 1.2 with concentrated HCl [43]. Furthermore, the sample was stirred using a magnetic stirrer (400 rpm, 37 °C), and 1 mL was withdrawn at intervals of 10, 30, 60, and 120 min. Digestion simulation was stopped by increasing the pH to 6.5 using 0.5 M ammonium bicarbonate (20 µL) to deactivate pepsin.

Furthermore, the digestion simulation resulting from 60 min in SGF was used as the starting material to simulate system stability in the small intestine. This test used simulated intestinal fluid (SIF) media containing 0.68% monopotassium phosphate, 1% pancreatin, and 3 mM sodium taurocholate, with pH adjusted to 6.8 [44]. Furthermore, the sample was stirred using a magnetic stirrer (400 rpm, 37 °C) for 30 min, and 1 mL sample was withdrawn at intervals of 10, 30, 60, 120, 240, and 360 min for further analysis. Each medium was added with 0.1% Tween 80 to maintain sink condition.

The release of calcein from the vesicles was evaluated by measuring the fluorescence intensity of calcein at an excitation wavelength of 490 nm and an emission wavelength of 520 nm using a Multimode Microplate Reader fluorometer instrument (GloMax®-Multi Detection System, Promega Corporation, Madison, USA). To calibrate the test, 100% leakage was achieved by adding Triton™ X-100 for 1 h at the end of incubation. The percentage of calcein leakage was calculated [44].

sec.title: In vivo evaluation of niosome absorption
sec.p: The in vivo evaluation study was approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Universitas Airlangga (Ethical Clearance No.: 2.KE.015.01.2023). UA niosome absorption was evaluated in the digestive tract with and without chitosan coating. To indicate the absorption of the niosome system in the digestive tract, 0.025% Nile red labeling was used as a fluorescence probe. Red fluorescence in the digestive tract indicated the degree of drug absorption. The formulation of UA niosomes labeled with Nile red was prepared by adding 0.025% Nile red solution to the mixture before evaporation of the organic solvent. The samples were then orally administered to the mice at 11 mg/kg body weight (BW), equivalent to UA. After 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, and 4 h, the mice were euthanized, and the stomach, duodenum, jejunum, and ileum segments were cryoembedded at –80 °C using the LEICA Tissue Freezing Medium.

Furthermore, the frozen intestine was cut into 10-µm slices (CM 3050S, Leica). Histological preparations were observed using a fluorescence microscope. Here, the intensity of drug absorption in the digestive tract was qualitatively compared between the formulas used and between the parts of the digestive tract to determine the region of maximum drug absorption in the digestive tract.

sec.title: Oral administration of UA niosomes in mice
sec.p: An in vivo biodistribution study of UA was performed using 6-week-old male Balb/c mice (Mus musculus). The Research Ethics Committee approved the animal experiments of the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Airlangga University, dated 16th May 2023, with Ethical Clearance No. 2.KEH.081.05.2023. All experiments complied with the ARRIVE guidelines. Mice were randomly divided into the following three groups: UA suspension, Nio-UA, and Nio-UA-CS. Mice were induced using a hepatocarcinogenic agent, N-nitrosodiethylamine, at a dose of 25 mg/kg BW weekly for 5 weeks. The samples were orally administered to mice at a dose equivalent to 16 mg UA/kg BW twice daily for 2d. On the third day, mice were euthanized, and their plasma and organs were collected [39, 46].

sec.title: Sample preparation and UA analysis in plasma and organs
Preparation of UA standard solutions in plasma matrix
sec.p: Samples for UA in plasma matrix were prepared by mixing 250 µL blood plasma with 50 µL of standard UA at several different concentrations. The mixtures were then acidified by adding 12 µL concentrated acetic acid. Extraction by vortexing was performed for 3 min using 3 mL of a mixture of n-hexane, dichloromethane, and 2-propanol (20:10:1 v/v/v), and the resulting material was centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was then transferred to a clean glass tube and dried overnight in a fume hood. The dry residue was added to 300 µL of methanol and vortexed for 60 s for complete dissolution. This preparation method was adapted from a previously described method with some modifications [47]. The supernatant was subsequently filtered through a 0.22-µm membrane and analyzed for UA content using HPLC.

sec.title: Preparation of UA standard solutions in an organ matrix
sec.p: UA was prepared in the organ matrix by homogenizing the organs in cold saline. For liver homogenization, the medium volume was approximately 5 mL, whereas for the heart, lungs, spleen, and kidneys, the volume was 2 mL. Homogenization was performed until the organs and normal cold saline mixture formed a uniform brownish liquid. Approximately 850 µL of organ matrix was placed in a glass tube and added to 150 µL of standard UA solution prepared at several concentrations. The mixtures were acidified by adding 40 µL concentrated acetic acid solution and further extracted for UA content using 6 mL of a hexane–dichloromethane–2–propanol mixture at respective volume ratios of 20:10:1. They were subsequently vortexed for approximately 3 min and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatants were transferred to clean glass tubes and dried in a fume hood. The residue was then dissolved in 400 µL of methanol using a method adapted from a previous report research with certain modifications [47]. The supernatant was filtered through a 0.22-µm membrane and analyzed for UA content using HPLC.

sec.title: HPLC analysis of UA levels
sec.p: For HPLC analysis, the sample volume was 20 µL. The stationary phase for sample analysis involved a Thermo SCIENTIFIC ODS Hypersil® column with dimensions of 4.6 × 150 mm, with a particle size of 5 µm. Two different mobile phases were used for sample analysis. The first mixture consisted of acetonitrile: 0.5% acetic acid solution (90:10 v/v) for UA assay in plasma, whereas the second was composed of acetonitrile: 0.5% acetic acid solution (70:30 v/v) for drug analysis in organ matrices. The flow rate was 1 mL/min, and the column temperature was set to 25 °C. HPLC featured a UV detector, and the UA content was measured at a wavelength of 210 nm [38]. System suitability tests were performed by injecting a standard working solution thrice to verify the stability of the chromatographic system (USP 40). The peak areas and retention times were further analyzed for method validation.

sec.title: System suitability
sec.p: System suitability testing is mandatory for ensuring drug quality analyzed using chromatographic methods, since various chromatographic parameters affect the analysis results even when chromatographic requirements are fulfilled [48]. HPLC system suitability was evaluated by determining UA retention time, peak area, resolution, theoretical plate, tailings, and asymmetry factor. In general, R ≥ 1.5, N ≥ 2000, and tailing factor As ≤ 1.5 are recommended for system suitability [49].

sec.title: Validation method
sec.p: The following characteristics were considered for validation of the HPLC analytical method: selectivity, linearity, accuracy, precision, limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ). Selectivity was evaluated to identify any substances potentially interfering with the analytes. Linearity was evaluated to determine the calibration curve with a regression line of the peak area versus the concentration of the standard solution. The accuracy was evaluated by injecting UA standard solutions prepared at three different concentrations and a clearly defined recovery percentage. Precision was evaluated by determining the coefficient of variation. The LOD represents the lowest detectable concentration of a substance, whereas LOQ is the lowest analyte concentration that can be measured using specific methods [49, 50].

sec.title: Selectivity
sec.p: Selectivity was evaluated by injecting UA prepared in the plasma and organ matrices under selected HPLC analytical conditions. The selective analytical method was indicated by the appearance of UA peaks without interference from the plasma matrix or organs. This method involved injecting a blank sample of the plasma matrix and an organ matrix devoid of UA analytes.

sec.title: Linearity
sec.p: Linearity was determined using a linear regression equation and the r-value following the injection of a working series of standard UA solutions prepared in the plasma and organ matrix at specific concentrations.

sec.title: Accuracy and precision
sec.p: Accuracy was determined using triplicate reporting % recovery, while precision employed six replications for % CV calculation, as follows ICH Q2 (R2) validation guidelines. Accuracy was evaluated by adding three different concentrations of UA to the plasma and organ matrix. Each concentration was analyzed in triplicate. The accuracy was evaluated by the %recovery value. A precision test was conducted by determining the relative standard deviation value, which is presented as the coefficient of variation (CV) [51].

sec.title: In vivo biodistribution study of UA niosomes with chitosan coating
sec.p: Mice were euthanized on the third day after cervical dislocation. First, mice were anesthetized using intraperitoneal ketamine 10 mg/mice. Blood samples from the inferior vena cava were collected using heparinized syringes, and the organs (heart, lung, liver, spleen, and kidney) were excised. To obtain plasma, blood was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm and 4 °C, with the supernatant being stored at –80 °C for further analysis. Mouse organs, including heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys, were excised and stored at –20 °C until further analysis.

The in vivo biodistribution of UA in mice in terms of drug levels in blood and organs was determined using HPLC and previously validated methods. Evaluation of plasma UA levels in the three groups (UA suspension, Nio-UA, and Nio-UA-CS) was performed using 300 µL of blood plasma acidified with 12 µL acetic acid. Subsequently, extraction was performed using 3 mL of the extraction solution. The mixture was then vortexed for 3 min, centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, transferred to a clean tube, and dried in a fume hood. Subsequently, the residue was dissolved in 300 µL of methanol pro-HPLC and vortexed for 60 s until the mixture dissolved homogeneously. The supernatant was then filtered using a 0.22-µm membrane and analyzed using HPLC to determine the UA content.

UA levels in the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys were evaluated by homogenizing the organs in 5 mL saline for the liver and 2 mL for the heart, lungs, spleen, and kidneys. Further, 1 mL of this sample was acidified with 40 µL acetic acid. Subsequently, extraction was performed using 6 mL of the extraction solution. The mixture was vortexed for 3 min and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was transferred to a clean tube and dried in a fume hood. The residue was then dissolved in 400 µL of methanol pro-HPLC and vortexed for 60 s until the mixture dissolved homogeneously. The supernatant was then filtered using a 0.22-µm membrane and analyzed using HPLC to determine the UA content.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All experiments were performed in replication, and data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using GraphPad Prism software version 9.0 (GraphPad Software). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was applied to compare multiple groups, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Characteristics of UA niosomes
sec.p:
Niosomes were characterized during the manufacture of UA niosome formulations to ensure that the niosomes formed were similar to those of the previously optimized formulation. The characterization parameters for UA niosomes included particle measurements, polydispersity index, ζ-potential, and encapsulation efficiency (%). Measurements were performed in triplicate using Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS. The results are shown in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
Characterization of Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS including A Particle size; B Polydispersity index; C ζ-potential; D Encapsulation efficiency. **p < 0.01; ****p < 0.0001

The findings of characterization revealed that chitosan coating of the UA niosome formulation could significantly increase the particle size (Fig. 1A). The average particle size of Nio-UA was 192.3 ± 7.3 nm, while that of chitosan-added noisome was 260.3 ± 20.5 nm. The polydispersity indices did not differ significantly between the chitosan-coated and non-coated niosome formulations (Fig. 1B). In contrast, ζ-potential analysis revealed that chitosan coating reduced the ζ-potential value of the Nio-UA-CS formula (–27.5 ± 1.29 mV) compared to that of the Nio-UA formula (–33.0 ± 1.40 mV) (Fig. 1C). Furthermore, the encapsulation efficiency (EE) of the Nio-UA formula was 37.51 ± 0.17%, which significantly decreased to 25.84 ± 0.32% on adding chitosan in the Nio-UA-CS formula (Fig. 1D).

sec.title: Solubility
sec.p:
Increase in the water solubility of UA was evaluated by comparing the solubilities of free UA, UA niosomes, and UA niosomes coated with chitosan. Evaluation was performed by adding UA at a saturated concentration and stirring for 24 h (Fig. 2A).Fig. 2
Evaluation of the (A) increase in solubility (B) Permeability due to LogP value of UA in water through formulation in a niosome system with and without chitosan coating (n = 3). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ****p < 0.0001

The LOD was first determined in this evaluation, which was 2.80 µg/mL, and the LOQ value was 8.49 µg/mL. Meanwhile, the free UA formula in water has a very low solubility below the LOD value; hence, it was not detected using HPLC in this study. However, after formulation in the niosome system at the same concentration (1 mg/mL UA dispersed in 4 mL water), its solubility in water increased compared to that in its free form. The encapsulation of UA in niosomes increased the solubility of UA from 1.02 × 10–4 mg/mL [10] to 23.49 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA and 22.34 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA-CS. These results confirmed that the niosome system formulation can significantly enhance the poor solubility of UA in water (*p < 0.05 and **p < 0.01). Chitosan coating on UA niosomes did not increase the solubility of UA (p > 0.05), indicating no significant difference between the two formulations.

sec.title: Permeability
sec.p: Increase in the permeability of UA was evaluated by comparing the LogP values of free UA, UA niosomes, and UA niosomes coated with chitosan (Fig. 2B). The data revealed that free UA had a very high LogP value of 5.18 ± 0.05, indicating very high lipophilicity; therefore, it was included in drugs with poor permeability. After formulation into the niosomal system, the partition coefficient decreased significantly (p < 0.0001). The LogP values of Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS were 1.70 ± 0.26 and 1.74 ± 0.30, respectively, indicating an increase in the permeability characteristics of UA due to formation of the niosome system. The presence of chitosan coating did not affect the increase in LogP values.

sec.title: Stability in simulated gastrointestinal fluid media
sec.p:
In this study, a liposome system was used to compare and determine the niosome system stability. Calcein, which fluorescence at an excitation wavelength of 490 nm and an emission wavelength of 520 nm, was used as a labeling agent. Following formulation of the niosome and liposome system, 3.4 mM of the calcein-labeling agent was used to evaluate the release of calcein in SGF and SIF media (Fig. 3).Fig. 3
Profile of calcein release in simulated gastric fluid and simulated intestinal fluid media continuously for 8 h (n = 3). *p < 0.05

Stability was evaluated by comparing the niosome system with the liposome system and its accessible form as a suspension. Determination of the % of calcein released revealed that the Nio-UA formula exhibited maximum stability relative to that of the other formulas (Fig. 3). The low cumulative percentage of calcein released indicated that the system was relatively stable and experienced the least degradation due to exposure to the digestive tract environment in SGF and SIF media. Other formulations, such as the liposome formulation, showed higher calcein release, indicating that the system was relatively less stable than the UA niosome formulation with chitosan coating. Thus, the Nio-UA-CS formula was more stable than the other systems. A mathematical model was applied to the data, and the results showed that the most appropriate model with an r value closest to 1 was the Korsmeyer–Peppas model.

sec.title: In vivo evaluation of drug absorption in the digestive tract
sec.p:
After oral administration, a drug travels through the stomach into the intestine. Some drugs are absorbed in the stomach. For absorption, orally administered drugs must be stable upon exposure to extreme pH and enzymes, which can degrade the drug. In vitro drug evaluation demonstrated that the niosomal system can be stabilized by exposure to the gastric fluid environment; therefore, the drug is expected to remain stable when administered orally. Drug absorption is shown in Fig. 4. The drug then enters the intestines and is absorbed in the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. The highest drug absorption occurred in the duodenum 4 h after drug administration. Drug absorbed in the jejunum was lesser than that in the duodenum. However, in the formulation with chitosan coating, qualitative drug absorption was relatively high in the jejunum. Thus, chitosan can increase drug absorption through the paracellular pathway and the mucoadhesive effect of chitosan, resulting in longer intestinal drug retention and enhanced drug absorption process.Fig. 4
Microscopic photographs of tissue slices from organs (gastric, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and liver) taken several hours after the oral administration of UA with Nile red labeling of the Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS groups. Red color indicates the fluorescence of Nile Red in niosomes accumulated in the organ. Scale bar= 100 µm

The drug then accumulates in the liver, which is the target organ for UA niosome therapy. Based on the results of photomicroscopy using a fluorescence microscope with a rhodamine filter, the distribution of UA niosomes in the liver of mice was marked by a red color called Nile red fluorescence. Drug accumulation in the liver was relatively high 4 h after oral administration. Qualitatively, a high fluorescence intensity difference was observed in the distribution of UA niosomes. The UA niosomes with chitosan coating showed a higher intensity than those without chitosan coating in the liver, suggesting that the chitosan-coated niosomes was more efficient in drug delivery to the liver via the oral route.

sec.title: Validation of the UA analysis method
sec.p:
For the selectivity test, blank plasma and organ tissue matrices were analyzed using HPLC. After 10 and 20 min of UA analysis in the plasma and organ matrices, respectively, no additional peaks appeared at the retention time corresponding to UA, indicating the absence of interfering peaks in the UA peak (Fig. 5). Thus, the analytical method exhibited a high level of selectivity. sec.title: In vivo biodistribution of UA
sec.p:
The results of the measurement of UA levels in the plasma samples and matrices of organs, including the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys, of mice administered the UA suspension, Nio-UA, and Nio-UA-CS are shown in Fig. 6. Based on plasma UA levels, the highest levels were observed in the Nio-UA-CS-treated group. However, no significant differences were observed in UA levels in the liver and spleen between the UA, Nio-UA, and Nio-UA-CS suspensions. In addition, UA was not detected in the lungs, heart, or kidneys. Thus, the chitosan coating promoted an increase in the drug levels in the blood. In addition, in terms of drug accumulation in organs, UA was concentrated in the liver, with minimal or undetectable drug levels in other organs.Fig. 6
Biodistribution profile of UA in plasma and organ matrices (including the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys) in various formulations, UA suspension, Nio–UA, and Nio–UA–CS

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: UA, a BCS class IV drug with poor solubility 1.02 × 10–4 mg/mL [10] and high lipophilicity, exhibits limited oral bioavailability. Niosome encapsulation increased its solubility 23-fold 23.49 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA and 22.34 × 10–3 mg/mL for Nio-UA-CS, attributed to UA entrapment within niosome bilayers due to their amphipathic properties. UA, which has a poor solubility, is trapped in the niosome bilayer membrane through interactions with the alkyl chains of the surfactant [20]. The hydrophilic polar groups on the external surface of the niosome form hydrogen bonds with water, thereby increasing drug solubility [20, 21]. In contrast, surfactants can increase the solubility of water and oil phases by reducing the interfacial tension between them [55]. Thus, the solubility of UA, which is poorly soluble in water, can be enhanced by encapsulating the drug in the bilayer membranes of niosomes.

Permeability across cell membranes is the key to absorption and distribution [56], ultimately affecting drug bioavailability [57]. Moreover, prior to intestinal absorption, the drug must penetrate the mucus barrier in the gastrointestinal tract, which restricts drug absorption. UA is attributed to their lipophilic nature (LogP = 7.92), which complicates drug penetration across biological membranes, resulting in the partitioning and retention of these compounds in the membrane [58, 59]. In general, drugs with higher LogP values (LogP >3) have difficulty in penetrating the mucus layer of the digestive tract, while those with lower P values (LogP <1) cannot be partitioned into the lipid membrane [60]. The Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS formulations exhibited LogP values of 1.70 ± 0.26 and 1.74 ± 0.30, respectively. Decrease in the LogP value of UA indicated that niosome formation increased in vitro drug permeability. Based on Lipinski’s rule of five standards, the formulation of UA in the niosomal system successfully enhanced the permeability of UA, making it an ideal drug for absorption in the digestive tract. This is due to the polar groups outside the niosome forming hydrogen bonds with water, which allows for increased drug partitioning. Additionally, cholesterol controls membrane permeability by inducing a conformational arrangement of lipid chains, which affects drug permeability [61]. In addition, surfactants increase drug permeability by disrupting the structural regularity of membrane components, thereby facilitating passive diffusion [62]. In addition, surfactants increase drug penetration into the gastrointestinal tract membrane, thereby increasing drug absorption [63]. This is because penetration-enhancing agents can increase paracellular and transcellular drug transport [64].

To evaluate the stability of the niosome system during oral administration, niosome stability evaluation was performed by comparing the niosome and liposome systems after in vitro exposure to gastrointestinal media. Upon oral administration, liposomes experience some physical and chemical instabilities, such as aggregation, fusion, or leakage during storage [65]. In vitro stability evaluation revealed that niosomes exhibited lower calcein release than liposomes (Fig. 3). Furthermore, chitosan increased niosome stability by decreasing calcein release, which is an effective index to characterize the biomembrane properties of nanovesicles [66]. In this study, Lipo-UA and Lipo-UA-CS showed the highest calcein release, which differed significantly from that of Nio-UA-CS. Liposomal phospholipids are unstable and easily degraded in the digestive tract [44]. Exposure to gastric acid and digestive enzymes can hydrolyze the phospholipid ester bonds, which form liposomes [67]. Bile salts solubilize liposomal membranes, making them more susceptible to attack owing to increased membrane fluidity. Pepsin and pancreatin can degrade the liposome membrane. Pepsin can hydrolyze and degrade liposomes, causing cargo leakage, which consequently inactivates or degrades the drugs encapsulated in liposomes [68, 69].

Among the polymers used for stability enhancement, chitosan has gained significant attention owing to its excellent stability in biological media [70]. Nanocomplex formulations using chitosan suggest that the drug remains stable when entering the stomach and small intestine, where chitosan potentially protects it from degradation in the gastrointestinal environment [71]. Consistently, in this study, we observed that chitosan coating provided the lowest calcein release, indicating that niosomes with chitosan coating are relatively stable compared to liposome formulations without chitosan coating. As alternatives to liposomes, which are easily degraded after exposure to the gastrointestinal environment, niosomes are considered chemically and physically stable [72]. When administered orally, niosomes are stable against exposure to SGF and SIF in the gastrointestinal tract.

The Nio-UA-CS formulation significantly increased the stability of niosomes in the gastrointestinal tract, with the lowest calcein release. Chitosan coating is essential for maintaining the stability of nanoparticles under pH variation, preventing premature drug release before reaching its target site [73]. Presumably, the chitosan coating forms a wall outside the niosome to inhibit drug release [36, 74]. In addition, chitosan nanoparticles are relatively stable at an acidic pH of 1.6–5.2 and do not disintegrate at pH 6–7.4 [75].

Drug absorption indicates the ability of a drug to penetrate the gastrointestinal tract. Drug absorption after oral administration occurs primarily in the intestine and is mainly controlled by the water solubility of the drug and its intestinal permeability. Drug fluorescence was relatively less in the stomach (Fig. 4), indicating that, in general, the drug was not absorbed in the stomach. Generally, absorption does not occur in the stomach since its surface area is smaller than that of the intestine [76]. In the stomach, the niosomal system remains intact, which is attributable to the stability of Nio-UA and Nio-UA-CS, which are relatively stable after exposure to SGF.

Pharmacotherapeutically, drugs administered orally for systemic purposes are absorbed in the small intestine [77]. During absorption, UA solubility in the digestive tract is critical. In this study, we used the labeling agent, Nile red, which is a hydrophobic dye [78]. Nile red in its free form is difficult to penetrate and produces poor fluorescence signals [78]. Thus, the drug entering the small intestinal epithelial cells is a form of niosome, which remains intact and labeled with Nile red. Based on these data, the highest drug absorption occurred in the duodenum 4 h after oral administration, as indicated by the highest drug fluorescence (Fig. 4). The duodenum has the largest surface area in the digestive tract with villi and microvilli [29].

Niosome modification with a chitosan coating also allows for a more effective mucoadhesive mechanism in the digestive tract [79] and extends the residence time of drugs in the intestine [80]. Chitosan can be added to increase the oral bioavailability of drugs with poor permeability; it functions as a permeation enhancer and a mucoadhesive, thus increasing the drug residence time at the absorption site. This mechanism is driven by the cationic surface charge, which electrostatically interacts with negatively charged mucus and cell membranes [81]. The underlying mechanism is that the electrostatic bond of nanoparticles on the chitosan coating can occur between the positive charge associated with the protonated amino group (NH3+) on chitosan and mucin, which is negatively charged because of the ionization of sialic acid at pH 6.8 [36]. Thus, the ability of chitosan to interact with negatively charged mucosal surfaces may potentially extend the residence time in the intestinal mucosa and improve the therapeutic performance of loaded drugs, such as UA [73]. Consistently, we observed the most optimal absorption in the proximal intestine, including the duodenum and jejunum. This was indicated by the high fluorescence in the jejunum after oral administration compared to that without chitosan coating. No absorption was observed in the ileum. The increased absorption of this drug further increases its bioavailability in the digestive tract [80].

A chitosan coating also allows membrane penetration [79]. This is because chitosan can trigger the opening of tight junctions (TJs) between epithelial cells and facilitate the paracellular transport of a drug formulated in the delivery system [80]. TJs form a barrier that allows the absorption of water and electrolytes but prevents the entry of inflammatory and infectious agents into systemic circulation. TJs comprise integral transmembrane protein complexes, including claudins, occludins, and junctional adhesion molecules [82]. Chitosan disrupts TJs through decreased expression, particularly that of claudin-4, via the translocation of TJ proteins from the membrane to the cytoskeleton, thus increasing penetration [83]. Consistently, drug accumulation in formulations with a chitosan coating exhibited higher absorption in the digestive tract.

Following penetration in intestinal epithelial cells, drugs accumulate at the target site, such as the liver. Based on the results obtained, the accumulation of Nio-UA-CS in the liver is qualitatively higher than that of Nio-UA after 4 h of oral administration. This is in accordance with the research conducted by Miatmoko et al. in [39], wherein the chitosan coating of niosome formulations qualitatively increased drug accumulation in the liver after oral administration. The stability of nanoparticles influences their accumulation in the body; this stability is also influenced by nanoparticle surface characteristics, such as the ζ-potential. Positively charged nanoparticles can cause non-specific adsorption and accumulate in several organs, such as the liver [84]. In the liver, particles generally accumulate in the Kupffer cells, hepatocytes, and endothelial cells [85].

A biodistribution study was conducted to determine the bioavailability of UA after oral administration using the niosome system in systemic circulation. The findings revealed that chitosan coating could increase plasma drug levels. This is because the biopharmaceutical properties of UA are altered when formulated as niosomes, where solubility, permeability, and residence time increase, thus increasing the absorption of UA. In addition, in terms of the nanoparticles used, the formulation of nano-sized drugs improves drug distribution, especially in the liver, due to the liver cancer animal model in this research. In cancer, tumor blood vessels are more permeable; therefore, molecules of a specific size tend to accumulate more in tumor tissues than in normal tissues. This phenomenon is now known as the enhanced permeation and retention EPR effect [86]. A size between 100–200 nm is recognized as the best particle size for the EPR effect, which is the main mechanism for the passive targeting of nanoparticles to tumor sites [87]. Hepatic drug accumulation is inseparable from the characteristics of sinusoids in the liver. Sinusoidal endothelial cells form a continuous layer along sinusoid blood vessels. UA levels in other organs were low or undetectable. It was absent in the spleen, heart, lungs, and kidneys, since it did not accumulate in these organs (Fig. 6).

Thus, the formulation of UA niosomes can overcome the problems of low solubility and permeability of UA through drug encapsulation in the niosome bilayer membrane. The stability of UA niosomes with chitosan coating increased the system stability during exposure to gastrointestinal tract media, suggesting the stability of the Nio-UA-CS formula after oral administration and entry into the gastrointestinal tract. Consequently, Nio-UA-CS can be absorbed optimally in the small intestine and accumulate in the liver. Increased drug absorption of the Nio-UA-CS formulation provides good drug biodistribution, indicated by higher plasma UA levels, which are higher than those in its free form. In addition, the formulation increases drug accumulation in the liver, which is the target organ of UA therapy in liver cancer. This overall characteristic improvement will potentially optimize UA use in liver cancer therapy.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Niosome formation increases the solubility and permeability of UA; chitosan coating further enhances the stability of UA niosomes in vitro. The chitosan coating of the niosome formulation can also increase the degree of UA absorption in the duodenum, jejunum, and ileal digestive tracts. Thus, niosomes with chitosan coating can increase the biodistribution of UA in plasma and hepatic accumulation in mice with liver cancer. The use of nanoparticles offers potential implications for improving the bioavailability of drugs for oral administration.
